title: America Can Build Again. Here’s How | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z's Matt Cronin argues America's inability to build stems from procedural over-process, chiefly NEPA and endless litigation, rather than democracy or environmental protection, citing cost and delay examples and peer countries that build fast. He urges Congress to pass bipartisan permitting reform (the Senate's 2026 act) built on limited review, hard deadlines, one review, final permits and categorical exclusions.

insights.claim: San Francisco's Noe Valley public toilet (150 sq ft) was projected at $1.7 million and over two years, versus the Golden Gate Bridge built in about four and a half years for $35 million, illustrating how far US building capacity has fallen.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Builds the narrative that process, not capability, is the binding constraint.

insights.claim: California high-speed rail has spent $13 billion of an original $33 billion budget with little to show, and estimated total cost has ballooned to $128 billion.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Flagship example of cost blowouts in US megaprojects.

insights.claim: In two decades America has completed only two large nuclear reactors from scratch, seven years late and roughly $23 billion over budget, versus four or five a year at the peak.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Nuclear scale-up faces a process and execution gap, not just a technology gap.

insights.claim: A 550-mile transmission line took 17 years, of which construction took two and legal battles the rest; a sister project took 15 years.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Grid buildout is gated by litigation, delaying electrification and AI-era power demand.

insights.claim: An Arizona copper mine that could supply a quarter of US copper demand has sat idle since its 1995 discovery, facing a 35-plus-year path to production due to permitting and litigation.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Critical-minerals supply security is hostage to permitting timelines.

insights.claim: US share of global manufacturing fell from 25% in 1997 to 16% today and, absent intervention, is projected to fall to 11% by 2030.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Frames permitting reform as an industrial-competitiveness issue.
insights.quote: America’s share of global manufacturing was 25% in 1997. It is 16% today. Absent intervention, it will fall to 11% by 2030.

insights.claim: Authoritarian speed is overstated: authoritarian states often reward raw output over profitability, producing unwanted assets such as China's ghost cities and industrial overcapacity dumped on global markets.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Challenges the view that China's model is simply superior at building.

insights.claim: Democracies can build fast under the right conditions: the US opened about half the Interstate system within a decade after the 1956 framework, Spain built 3,800+ km of high-speed rail cheaply, and Taiwan brings fabs online in roughly two years via one-stop administration.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Provides replicable templates for reform rather than regime change.

insights.claim: Regime type is not the decisive variable for building; clear authority, standardized requirements, predictable financing, competent agencies and rules forcing decisions are.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Policy design, not governance system, determines build speed.
insights.quote: Regime type is not the decisive variable.

insights.claim: Blocking factories in the US does not cut emissions but exports them to dirtier producers such as China, which emits two to three times more carbon per unit of output than America.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Procedural obstruction can be net-negative for the climate.
insights.locator: Environmental Safety is Not the Problem

insights.claim: Peers prove strong environmental protection and speed coexist: Canada and Australia permit mines up to five times faster, Madrid expanded its metro cheaply, and Switzerland finished the Alps rail tunnel a year early.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Benchmarks for reform: substantive standards, minimal procedural delay.

insights.claim: The winning model consolidates environmental studies into a single permit, has courts review legality rather than relitigate analysis, uses short challenge clocks, and lets losers bear winners' costs to deter frivolous suits.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Concrete design pattern for permitting regimes.

themes.theme: NEPA and litigation as the core problem

insights.claim: NEPA is purely procedural, and layered regulation plus aggressive litigation turned it into a tool to thwart construction; in 2024 environmental assessments averaged over a year and EISs nearly four years, with mean EIS cost of $6.6 million per DOE data.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Quantifies the permitting tax that deters capital before it deploys.
insights.quote: a modest procedural requirement into a blunt and haphazard tool

insights.claim: Lack of permit finality is the key investment deterrent: clearing one review gives no certainty because opponents can bring another challenge, so threat of litigation alone kills projects at inception.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Capital formation, not just timelines, is the casualty; finality is worth pricing.

insights.claim: Cape Wind, a 468 MW offshore wind project, was abandoned after 15+ years and over $100 million without a single turbine, showing process obstruction hurts clean energy too.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Climate and process-reform goals align.

insights.claim: More than 2,000 GW of capacity, nearly twice the existing US power fleet, sits in an interconnection queue averaging about five years per project.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Power supply for data centers and electrification is gated by queue process.

insights.claim: The regulatory maze is self-perpetuating: only large firms can navigate it, and an ecosystem of attorneys, accountants and consultants profits from keeping it standing, taxing innovators twice and pushing firms abroad.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Reform faces entrenched rent-seeking, favoring incumbents over new entrants.

insights.claim: The author backs the Senate's Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 and similar House bills, noting an unusual coalition of petrochemical executives, renewable advocates, builders and bankers supports permitting reform.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
entities: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026
insights.so_what: Legislative momentum for permitting reform is bipartisan and a potential catalyst for energy and infrastructure build.

insights.claim: Five priorities: limit procedural review (build while NEPA errors are fixed, expedite judicial review, loans alone don't trigger NEPA), hard deadlines with enforcement, one project one review with a lead agency, permit finality with no injunctions for procedural errors, and expanded categorical exclusions including grid and storage.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Checklist for evaluating whether a final bill actually moves build timelines.

insights.claim: Federal-state partnerships that pre-clear sites for environmental review, utilities and zoning could let companies build in weeks rather than years, as Taiwan does.
insights.speaker: Matt Cronin
insights.so_what: Pre-cleared industrial sites could be a major lever for reshoring.
